opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we hear constantly from customers. For a long time, regulated industries like financial services, healthcare, government, and telecom have been cautious about the cloud. They've moved some workloads there, but their most sensitive data, like patient records, transaction histories, and proprietary models, has largely stayed on-prem or in tightly controlled environments.

AI amplifies that tension. To get real value from generative AI, you have to feed these models your most valuable data. You're not just storing it anymore. You're running inference on it, fine-tuning on it, and building retrieval pipelines around it. For a bank or a hospital, the idea of shipping all that to a third-party API is a non-starter in a lot of cases, whether because of compliance, data residency rules, or just institutional risk tolerance.

So what we're seeing is a real pull toward bringing AI to the data rather than the data to the AI. Enterprises want to run inference in their own data centers, at the edge, or in sovereign or private clouds where they keep control. That's a big shift from the first wave of generative AI, which was very centralized around a few hyperscalers.

The challenge is that inference at scale has historically been really expensive and power-hungry. Most enterprise data centers weren't built to host racks of GPUs drawing enormous amounts of power. That's a big part of why we started d-Matrix the way we did. We focused specifically on inference efficiency, using approaches like digital in-memory compute to cut the energy and cost per token so that running these models on-prem becomes practical, not just theoretically possible.

So I'd say AI doesn't make regulated companies less worried about the cloud. If anything, it sharpens those concerns. But it's also forcing the infrastructure to evolve so they don't have to choose between using cutting-edge AI and keeping control of their data. I think over the next few years you'll see a much more hybrid world, where training might happen centrally but a huge share of inference moves closer to where the sensitive data actually lives.

r001.rationale: The response says AI “amplifies” the tension and “sharpens” concerns, indicating they have intensified rather than stating they have not materially changed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the short answer is that AI has actually made those concerns sharper, not softer, and that's a healthy thing.

If you go back five or six years, the cloud conversation for a bank or a hospital or a defense contractor was mostly about storage and compute. Where does the data sit, who has the keys, can I pass my audit. Those are hard problems, but they're well-understood problems, and the big cloud providers built very good answers to them.

AI changes the shape of the question. Now it's not just "where does my data live," it's "what is my data being used to teach." When you send proprietary records into a model that someone else operates, you're not just storing bits, you're potentially contributing to a system whose behavior you don't control and can't fully inspect. For a regulated company, that's a very different risk posture. A compliance officer can read a data-residency contract. It's much harder to reason about what a model has absorbed.

So what we're seeing is a kind of bifurcation. There's a class of workloads, general productivity, drafting, summarization of public material, where companies are perfectly comfortable using hosted frontier models. And then there's a class of workloads touching patient data, trading data, customer PII, where the instinct is increasingly to bring the model to the data instead of the other way around. Run inference on premises, or at the edge, or in a sovereign environment, so the sensitive data never leaves a boundary you control.

What's made that possible is that inference has gotten dramatically cheaper and more efficient to deploy. You no longer need a hyperscaler's footprint to run a very capable model. That shifts the economics, and once the economics shift, the regulatory instinct, which was always to keep things close, suddenly becomes practical rather than just aspirational.

I'd also say regulators themselves are catching up fast. In Europe especially, but also in sectors like finance in the US, the expectation is moving toward explainability and data lineage. If you can't say where the data went and what touched it, that's going to be a problem regardless of how good the model is.

So my view is that AI is forcing the cloud question to mature. It's less "cloud or not cloud" and more "which workloads belong where, and how do I keep control of the pieces that matter." The companies that figure that out early are going to move faster, not slower, because they'll have a clear framework instead of a blanket fear.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI has made concerns “sharper” and changed the shape of the cloud question, directly contradicting the claim that AI has not materially changed them.

astra-6.text:
I think AI is going to make those concerns even more significant. For a regulated company, its data is often both its most valuable asset and its most sensitive asset. If you’re a bank or a healthcare organization, you want the benefits of AI, but you also need control over where that data goes and who can access it.

So I think we’ll see more demand for bringing AI to the data. That might mean running models on premises or in a private cloud, rather than sending sensitive information to an external service. The cloud will still have a role, but companies will want more flexibility about where they run their models, particularly when they move from experimenting with AI to using it in everyday operations.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will make those concerns “even more significant,” rather than saying AI has not materially changed longstanding concerns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI is making those concerns much more concrete. A regulated company wants to use its proprietary data to get better answers, but that’s also the data it’s most concerned about sending outside its own environment. Where does it go? Who can access it? Is it being used to train somebody else’s model?

So I don’t think this is simply a choice between adopting AI and keeping your data secure. Companies are going to want more flexibility in where they run these models—whether that’s in a private cloud or on premises—and more control over what happens to their data. The opportunity is to bring AI to the data, so they can get the benefit without having to move everything somewhere else.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is making concerns about sending data to the cloud “much more concrete,” rather than stating that AI has not materially changed longstanding concerns.
